abstract: General matrix multiplication in DNN training must accommodate uneven dimensions and unstructured zeros. A fixed systolic shape can therefore leave multipliers unused while still executing zero operations. We present SIGMA, which makes operand distribution and partial-sum reduction flexible enough for independently sized dot products to share an array. A bitmap guides placement of useful operands; a Benes multicast fabric feeds Flexible Dot Product Engines (Flex-DPEs), and the Forwarding Adder Network (FAN) routes their partial sums. Multiple Flex-DPEs form a Flex-DPU for each GEMM. A cycle-based analytical evaluation uses dimensions and sparsities from GNMT, Transformer, NCF, and DeepBench, with all modeled accelerators scaled to 16,384 PEs and the better of weight-stationary and input-stationary mappings reported for SIGMA. On sparse irregular workloads, the study reports 5.7× speedup over TPU-like systolic designs and approximately 3× over compared sparse accelerators adapted to GEMMs. These are modeled GEMM results, not full training runs. In a 28 nm post-layout comparison at 500 MHz with BF16 multiplication and FP32 addition, flexibility raises compute-array area by 37.7%. SIGMA occupies 65.10 mm² and consumes 22.33 W, excluding large SRAMs. Bandwidth and repeated operand streaming remain limiting factors; Eyeriss v2 is faster on two evaluated GEMMs.
introduction: General matrix multiplication is a central computation in the DNN training workloads considered here, but its dimensions and useful work do not always match a fixed compute array. Uneven matrix dimensions can leave part of a systolic array idle, while unstructured zeros can consume operations without contributing to the result. Keeping an operand stationary does not by itself resolve either mismatch: the machine must place useful products on available multipliers and combine them into dot products of the required sizes. The design problem therefore extends beyond stationary utilization. Overall efficiency also depends on whether distribution and reduction can accommodate irregular work without stranding arithmetic resources.

Reconfigurable dataflow and sparse computation provide relevant starting points. MAERI addresses flexible dataflow mapping through reconfigurable interconnects [kwon2018maeri], while SCNN targets compressed-sparse convolutional networks [parashar2017scnn]. For training GEMMs, SIGMA couples flexible allocation of useful multiplications with flexible formation of their sums. It groups a logical row of multipliers into Flexible Dot Product Engines, or Flex-DPEs. A bitmap identifies zero positions and guides useful-operand placement; a Benes distribution fabric multicasts operands to the multipliers that need them. The Forwarding Adder Network (FAN) routes partial sums so that independently sized dot products can share the reduction fabric. Multiple Flex-DPEs compose into a Flex-DPU for a GEMM. Together, these choices let operand placement and reduction follow the available useful work instead of requiring every dot product to occupy the same fixed shape.

We evaluate SIGMA with a cycle-based analytical model and a SCALE-sim systolic baseline, scaling each modeled accelerator to 16,384 PEs. The GEMMs use dimensions and sparsities from GNMT, Transformer, NCF, and DeepBench; SIGMA reports the better of weight-stationary and input-stationary mappings. Comparisons extend EIE, SCNN, OuterSPACE, Eyeriss v2, Packed Systolic, and Cambricon-X to GEMMs and explore alternative matrix orientations and sparsity placements. The study reports 5.7× speedup over TPU-like systolic designs on sparse irregular workloads and approximately 3× over the compared sparse accelerators. These results concern GEMMs rather than complete training execution. Flexibility also has a physical cost: post-layout compute arrays in commercial 28 nm technology at 500 MHz, using BF16 multiplication and FP32 addition, occupy 65.10 mm² and consume 22.33 W for SIGMA, versus 47.27 mm² and 12.25 W for the systolic array. The 37.7% area increase excludes large SRAMs, as do both power figures. Operand supply remains a constraint: Eyeriss v2 is faster on two GEMMs because it retains both operands locally while SIGMA streams one repeatedly. Streaming sparsity and bandwidth thus delimit the benefit of flexible compute allocation.
